client: I've been really stressed out about this family reunion that's coming up next month, and honestly just thinking about it makes my heart race. There was this whole fallout with my cousin last year, and I don't know how to be in the same room as them without it turning into a disaster. I'm not even sure talking about it here is going to change anything, because the situation feels pretty out of my control.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that your heart races just thinking about it — anticipating a difficult encounter with someone you've had a real falling-out with is genuinely stressful, and your feelings are valid. I also hear that part of you feels a little skeptical that talking will help, and I want to gently hold space for that doubt while also wondering if we might discover some small things that *are* within your control, even in a situation that feels overwhelming. 

What do you imagine the worst moment at the reunion might look like, and what does the version of you in that moment need most?

client: I think the worst moment would be if she just looks right through me, like I don't even exist, or worse, if she says something cutting in front of everyone and I just freeze up and can't respond. What I'd need in that moment is probably just to not fall apart, to not let everyone see how much it still hurts. But honestly, I'm not sure there's anything I can do to prepare for that, because when I'm in it, my mind just goes blank and all the things I told myself I'd say disappear.
therapist: That image of freezing and going blank is so human — it's your nervous system going into protection mode, not a personal failure or weakness. What's really interesting is that underneath your fear of "falling apart," there seems to be a belief that if others see your hurt, something terrible will happen — and I'd love to gently explore whether that's actually true. What do you imagine people would think or do if they *did* see that this situation affects you?

client: I guess... I imagine they'd think I was weak, or that I couldn't handle things. Like, people at work especially — if they saw me get emotional or struggle, I feel like they'd lose respect for me, or start questioning whether I'm actually competent. It's almost like I've built this image of being the person who has it together, and if that cracks even a little, I'm terrified the whole thing just collapses.
therapist: That fear of the "whole thing collapsing" if one crack shows is such a heavy weight to carry — it's like you've been holding yourself to a standard where you're only safe if you're perfectly composed, all the time. I'm curious about that belief though, because I wonder if you've ever actually seen someone you respect show vulnerability, and whether it truly made you think *less* of them. What evidence do you have, from your own experience, that emotional moments really do destroy how others see a person?

client: I mean... yeah, I can think of a few people I respect who've broken down or admitted they were struggling, and I didn't think less of them. If anything, I remember feeling closer to them, like they trusted me with something real. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself, it just doesn't stick — it's like there's this voice that says "that's different, those are other people, you don't get the same allowance."
therapist: You just noticed something really important — that you extend grace and even *admiration* to others for their vulnerability, but there's a voice that puts you in a separate, harsher category, and that double standard is worth paying attention to. In CBT we'd call that an automatic thought, and the fact that you can already see it clearly ("that's different, that's other people") is actually the first step in loosening its grip. I'm wondering — where do you think that voice learned that *you* specifically don't get the same allowance as everyone else?

client: I've been sitting with that question and honestly it makes me uncomfortable, because I think I know the answer but saying it out loud feels like making excuses. Growing up, showing weakness or needing help was treated like a burden to other people, so I learned pretty early that my struggles were supposed to stay hidden. I guess that voice has been around so long I stopped questioning whether it was actually true or just something I absorbed.
therapist: What you just shared took real courage, and I want to gently push back on one word — calling this "making excuses" when really you're doing something much more honest, which is tracing where a belief came from so you can decide if it still serves you. That voice wasn't born from truth; it was a survival strategy a younger version of you developed to avoid feeling like a burden, and it made sense *then* — but you're not that child anymore, and you get to question whether it belongs in your life now. What might it feel like to experiment, even in a small and safe way, with letting one person see a little of what you're carrying?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that framing, but it still feels uncomfortably close to making excuses to me. Like, if I let someone see what I'm carrying and they pull away or get tired of it, that just confirms everything I already fear. I guess the honest answer to your question is that it feels terrifying, because the one person I'd trust enough to try that with is my friend Mara, and I don't want to risk losing that friendship over my problems.
therapist: The fact that Mara's name came so readily tells me that friendship already holds something really precious and trust-filled for you, and it makes sense that you'd want to protect it fiercely. But I want to reflect something back gently — you're predicting that sharing with Mara *will* lead to her pulling away, and yet you also told me earlier that when people you respected showed vulnerability, you felt *closer* to them, not burdened. What do you actually know about Mara, specifically, that would help us test whether that fear is a fact or a prediction?

client: That's... a fair point, and I hate that it's a fair point. When I actually think about Mara specifically, she's the one who called me three times when her dad was sick because she needed someone to talk to, and I showed up for that without thinking twice. But there's still this voice in my head saying that's different, that being the one who needs help is a completely different position, and I'm not sure I trust that the same rules apply to me.
therapist: It's so telling that your mind immediately went to "that's different" again — that voice is very practiced at finding reasons why you're the exception, isn't it? But notice what you just described: Mara needed you repeatedly, and not only did you not think less of her, you showed up without hesitation — and I'd gently ask whether you think Mara sees herself as weaker than you, or just as someone who trusted you enough to let you in. What do you think it would mean to Mara if you gave her the same chance to show up for you that she gave you?

client: I mean... when you put it that way, I guess I never thought about it from Mara's side like that. Maybe she would want the chance to be there for me the way I was for her, and maybe I've been kind of taking that away from her by always keeping things surface level. But it still feels really scary, like what if I reach out and she's busy or doesn't respond the way I hope, and then I feel even more alone than I do now?
therapist: That fear of reaching out and feeling *more* alone afterward is real and worth taking seriously — and it also makes sense that your nervous system would rather avoid the risk than chance that pain. But I want to notice something with you: right now you're protecting yourself from a *possible* disappointing response from Mara, while the loneliness you're trying to avoid is already here, happening today. What would a very small, low-stakes first step toward Mara look like — something that feels more like testing the water than diving in?

client: I hear what you're saying, and logically it makes sense — the loneliness is already there, so what do I have to lose, right? But it's not that simple, because right now the loneliness feels like a dull ache I can manage, and if I reach out to Mara and she's distant or gives me some half-hearted response, it turns into something sharper, more like a confirmation that I'm just not someone people really want around. I guess a low-stakes thing might be sending her a meme or something casual, but even that feels weirdly exposing, like I'd be watching my phone waiting for her to respond and reading everything into how long it takes.
therapist: You've just described something really insightful — that the dull ache feels *safer* because it's familiar and predictable, while hope feels dangerous because it opens the door to sharper pain, and that's a completely understandable way your mind has learned to protect you. I also want to gently name what's happening when you imagine watching your phone and reading into her response time — that's your mind already jumping to interpret neutral information as rejection, before anything has even happened. What if, just as a small experiment, you decided in advance what a "good enough" response from Mara would look like — not perfect, just enough to remind you that the connection is real?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it — like, intellectually I understand that I'm already setting myself up to see rejection even before she responds. But when you ask me to decide in advance what "good enough" looks like, I honestly don't know if I can do that, because my brain just moves the goalposts the second I get her actual response. Like, I'll tell myself "okay, if she replies within a few hours, that's fine," and then she replies in two hours and I'm already thinking "but her message was short, so she's probably pulling away."
therapist: What you're describing — the goalposts moving no matter what she does — tells me that the fear isn't really about Mara's response at all, but about a deeper belief that the evidence against your worth will always outweigh the evidence for it, so your mind keeps searching until it finds something that confirms what it already fears. That's exhausting, and it also means no response from Mara could ever fully feel like "enough" until that underlying belief starts to shift — which is actually really important information. I'm wondering, when you imagine the version of you who *didn't* need Mara's response to be a certain way to feel okay, what would that person believe about themselves that you don't quite believe yet?
